```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
data(penguins)
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep), !is.na(body_mass))
```

## Learning Outcomes

Yesterday: one `.qmd` → a branded PDF. Today, the other axis: **one file to many**. You will be able to:

- **structure** several `.qmd` into one Quarto **project** with shared config (`_quarto.yml`);
- **build** a navigable, **branded website** — within-page cross-references, reproducible builds;
- **produce a publishable folder**, put it online, and explain how **freeze** lets it rebuild
  without re-running R.

By the end: the same penguins data, a set of pages (**including yesterday's report**) grown into a
**website your team can publish**.

::: notes
- **Frame:** Day 1 took one `.qmd` all the way to a branded PDF. Day 2 is the other axis — one file
  to many, tied together by config, then shipped. This is the machinery behind your team project's
  site.
:::

# Part 1 — Build & structure a project {.center}

From one file to a whole site.

## Why a *project*? {#why-project}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
Open your editor: from here we build one project together.
:::

One `.qmd` renders alone. A **project** is a folder Quarto treats as one unit (shared config, one
build, one output folder):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
# at the project root
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site  # everything renders here
format:
  html:
    toc: true          # set once, every page gets it
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- `quarto render` builds the **whole** folder, not one file.
- Header options set **once** apply to every page.
- **`output-dir`** — the folder the built site lands in (`_site` by default). Publish *that*.
:::
:::
::::

::: aside
Quarto uses the **nearest `_quarto.yml`** up the tree as the project root: you add one to
`day2-projects/`, and nothing sits above it, so that folder *is* your project.
:::

::: notes
- **Say:** "Day 1 was one file. Today: many files, one project. Open your editor — we build one together."
- **Do:** show a minimal `_quarto.yml` — `project: type: website` + `output-dir`. "This folder is now one unit; `render` builds all of it, not one file."
- **Say (relevance):** the team project is many pages — this is how they connect.
:::

## Directory metadata — `_metadata.yml` {#metadata}

Yesterday a header set the defaults and a cell overrode them. `_metadata.yml` is that **same idea,
one scope wider**: options for every page in a **folder**, so you don't repeat them in each header:

``` {.yaml filename="analysis/_metadata.yml"}
# applies to every .qmd in analysis/
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
```

Same narrow-wins rule, now across files: **document header** > `_metadata.yml` > `_quarto.yml`.
Set defaults wide, override narrow.

::: aside
Today's lab project is flat (a couple of pages at the root), so there's no folder to scope. Reach for
`_metadata.yml` when a **subfolder** of pages shares options.
:::

::: notes
- **Callback (don't re-teach):** they learned header-vs-cell precedence yesterday (`#execution`).
  Don't re-derive "defaults wide, override narrow" — just widen it to the file/folder/project scope.
- **Say:** "Same rule as yesterday's header-beats-nothing / cell-beats-header — now a folder file
  sits between the page and the project."
:::

## Websites — pages & navigation {#websites}

You already set `type: website`, which makes the folder a **site**: its pages share one navbar and
sidebar. You describe that navigation once, and Quarto builds it:

``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
website:
  title: "Penguin Lab"
  # top bar — one entry per page
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
  # side menu, built from the files
  sidebar:
    contents: auto
```

. . .

`contents: auto` even builds the sidebar from the folder, so you don't hand-list pages.

::: {.aside}
**Listings** turn a folder of pages into an auto-generated index (a blog, a gallery of reports) via
`listing:` on a page. One slide's worth, more in the linked resources.
:::

::: notes
- **Do:** add the `website:` block live — navbar + sidebar — render, show the nav appear.
- **Say:** "You declare the nav once: the navbar you list, the sidebar `contents: auto` builds from the files — Quarto generates both."
- **Say (sets up next slide):** "each page renders on its own — that independence is exactly why cross-refs behave differently across pages."
- **Helpers:** flag the classic trap now — links are relative to the *source*, not `_site` — so they meet it before the lab.
:::

## Cross-references across a project {#xrefs}

::: {.callout-warning title="Eyes up — not a live *Follow along*"}
The next few slides are concept, no need to type along.
:::

Within **one page**, `@fig-`, `@tbl-`, `@eq-` resolve to a numbered, linked reference, exactly as
on Day 1. (Section headings work the same way with `@sec-`.)

. . .

Across **different website pages**, they do **not** auto-number: a website renders each page on its
own, so link between pages with ordinary Markdown links and the **navbar/sidebar** instead:

``` markdown
See the [analysis page](analysis.qmd) for the model.
```

::: {.callout-note title="Project-wide numbering is a *book*"}
If you need "Figure 3.2" to resolve *across* chapters, that's `type: book`: Quarto renders a book as
one unit with global numbering. A **website** keeps per-page numbering.
:::

::: notes
- **Pre-flight (not spoken):** if unsure on your installed Quarto, test one cross-page `@fig-`
  before the session — historically a website does not resolve it. Keep that check off the slide.
:::

## One brand → the whole project: `_brand.yml` {#brand}

Yesterday, `_brand.yml` branded one **Typst PDF**. Drop that **same file at the project
root** and Quarto **auto-discovers** it (no header line, no per-page config):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
``` {.yaml filename="_brand.yml"}
color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans
```
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
- **Every page and every deck** inherits it from that one root file, so you never name it in a page.
- Add a page later? Branded on render, nothing to wire up.
- Need an exception? `brand: false` opts a page out; `brand: other.yml` points it elsewhere.
:::
::::

::: notes
- **Callback (don't re-derive):** they saw this file yesterday, branding the PDF. Today's *new* angle is
  **scale** — one root file themes the whole multi-page project. Widen the scope; don't re-teach the file.
- **Hold back the theme-layer rule.** It used to be an aside on this slide. It is now the lab's
  brand step (Part 1, "Brand it"): they add `_brand.yml`, the fonts change, the colors don't, and
  working out why is the exercise. Saying "`brand` goes last, later layers win" here turns that step
  back into transcription. If someone asks outright, answer with the question instead: "what order do
  you think Quarto puts them in?"
- **Do:** show the site before / after dropping `_brand.yml` at the root — navbar + links go teal
  in one re-render. **Check your demo project first:** a bare `theme: cosmo` outranks the brand and
  the demo shows nothing. The theme list needs `brand` last (`theme: [cosmo, brand]`), or no
  `theme:` at all. Fix it silently before the session; don't narrate the fix.
- **Say:** "You saw this yesterday. Put it at the project root and every page *and* deck inherits it
  — brand once, not per file."
- **R plots (only if asked):** a plot still needs `theme_brand_ggplot2()` — same as yesterday; the
  lab's stretch covers it.
- **Escape hatch (if asked):** `brand: false` opts a page out; `brand: other.yml` points it
  elsewhere — the default brands everything, these are the overrides.
- **Precision:** "every page/deck" = every *supported-format* output (html, revealjs, typst,
  dashboard); an unsupported format just isn't branded — don't say "every output".
- **Placement:** this is Part-1 project config, not the Part-2 tail.
- **Helpers:** the lab installs `brand.yml` with `install.packages()` (not `pak`).
:::

# Part 2 — Scale & ship {.center}

Make builds reproducible, then publish: how your team ships its project.

::: notes
- **Welcome back** (after the break): "Before the break you built a branded, navigable site. Now we make its builds *reproducible* — freeze + renv — then ship it."
- One-sentence recap; don't re-teach Part 1.
:::

## Freeze — don't re-run the slow stuff {#freeze}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
Back in your project's `_quarto.yml`.
:::

**freeze** was one line in Day 1. Here it is in full. Compute can be slow: you don't want every
prose edit to re-run a 20-minute model fit. Two tools, easily confused:

::: {.incremental}
- **`cache`** — the **compute engine's** cache, not Quarto's: it defers to *knitr* (R) / *Jupyter Cache*.
  Per-**cell**, kept until that cell's code changes, and it works in a **single document**.
- **`freeze`** — **Quarto's** own switch, *not* about compute: it sets *when* a document re-executes.
  **Project-only**: rendering one file always runs it. Results live in `_freeze/`, refreshed only
  when its source changes. Commit it and **CI** *(the automated build)* rebuilds with **no R at all**.
:::

. . .

``` yaml
# _quarto.yml
execute:
  freeze: auto        # re-execute a document only when its source changes
```

That's `freeze: auto`, the setting to adopt: a page re-runs only when its own source changes. **`freeze: true`**
hands you full control instead → next slide.

::: notes
- **Say (motivation):** "Compute can be slow — you don't want a prose typo to re-run a 20-minute model fit." *(Localize to the room: a sequence alignment, a long MCMC, a big simulation.)*
- **Do:** the contrast is the point — **cache** = the *engine's* cache (knitr for R / Jupyter Cache), per-cell, works in a single doc; **freeze** = *Quarto's* switch, project-only, re-executes a doc only when its source changes. (Verified vs quarto.org `docs/projects/code-execution.html`.) Protect this distinction.
- **Do:** show `freeze: auto` in `_quarto.yml`; "re-runs a page only when *that page* changed."
- **If asked — why not just cache everything?** cache is per-cell and can go stale across a shared repo; freeze commits whole-document results for reproducible, R-free CI rebuilds. Different jobs.
- **Say (payoff):** commit `_freeze/` and **CI** *(a build that runs on every push)* rebuilds the site with **no R at all**.
- **Teaser:** the next slide is `freeze: true` — the render-on-demand workflow.
:::

## The freeze workflow — you hold the trigger {#freeze-workflow}

With **`freeze: true`**, a project build **never runs R**: it always reuses `_freeze/`. You refresh a
page only when you choose to, by rendering that one file (a single-file render always executes):

``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
execute:
  freeze: true
```

``` bash
quarto render analysis.qmd     # runs the code, rewrites _freeze/ — commit it with your change
```

. . .

The loop: **edit a page → render that one file → commit `_freeze/`**. The project build and **CI**
stay **R-free**: only the page you touched recomputes. That's exactly how **quarto.org** itself
is built.

. . .

`freeze: auto` instead lets the *build* recompute any changed (or not-yet-frozen) page. Convenient,
but `true` keeps the trigger in your hands.

::: notes
- **Anchor (real):** quarto.org runs `freeze: true` — verified in `quarto-dev/quarto-web/_quarto.yml`;
  contributors render the changed file locally and commit `_freeze/`, enforced by a `check-freeze.sh`
  git hook — the *same* discipline this workshop repo uses.
- **Say:** "true = the build never runs R; *you* decide when a page recomputes, by rendering it directly."
- **Do:** edit a cell on `analysis.qmd` → `quarto render analysis.qmd` → show `_freeze/` change + the
  timestamp tick; a full project render leaves it untouched.
- **Contrast (lab uses `auto`):** `auto` = the build recomputes changed pages for you (the setting you want,
  what the lab sets); `true` = deterministic CI + manual refresh (the CI mode).
- **If asked:** a `production` render profile can set `freeze: false` to force a full re-execution.
:::

## Reproducibility has two parts {#renv}

`freeze` pins the **results**. It doesn't pin **what produced them** (the package versions):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **`freeze`** → `_freeze/` — *"don't re-run the slow compute."*
- **`renv.lock`** → *"pin the packages, so the team rebuilds the same environment."*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
``` r
renv::init()       # once, to start tracking
renv::snapshot()   # write renv.lock
renv::restore()    # rebuild the same env
```
:::
::::

Together: a colleague (or CI) rebuilds the *same* site, with or without re-running the analysis.

::: notes
- **Timing:** renv is the first thing to drop if short on time — the cache-vs-freeze contrast is the point of this beat, protect that.
- **Say:** "freeze pins the *results*; renv.lock pins *what produced them* — the package versions. You want both."
:::

## Publishing {#publishing}

The hands-on part is small: **render, then point a host at `output-dir`.**

``` bash
quarto render              # builds the whole project into _site/
```

- `_site/` is the whole deliverable. Point any static host at it (an internal server, your
  department's pages, a hosting service).
- **Posit Connect Cloud** takes it in one command, with a free account and **no repository**:

``` bash
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud
```

The first run opens a browser to sign in, then uploads the folder you just built.

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn — optional, if we have time"}
Publish your site and open it on your phone. The lab has the steps. Everyone still leaves with
`_site/`, which is the deliverable either way.
:::

::: notes
- **Do:** show it live on this repo (`quarto publish posit-connect-cloud`). It is one command and a
  browser sign-in, so it *is* watchable, unlike a Pages build.
- **Say:** "You already made the thing you publish. `_site/` is the deliverable — this just puts it
  on a URL."
- **Prerequisite (say it early, on Day 1 if you remember):** a free Posit account. Anyone without
  one skips this and loses nothing.
- **Why not GitHub Pages:** we never taught git or GitHub, and the whole setup is built on not
  needing them (`use_course()`). Connect Cloud needs no repository.
- **If asked about automation:** yes, this can rebuild on a schedule or from a repo. That is the
  same CI story as the freeze beat, and it is a pointer, not a demo.
:::

## What you can do now {#wrap-up}

You can now:

- structure `.qmd` into a **project** — `_quarto.yml`, `output-dir`, `_metadata.yml`;
- build a **branded website** with navigation, and know why cross-page refs differ from a book;
- make builds **reproducible** (`freeze` + `renv.lock`), produce a **publishable `_site/`** for a host
  or CI, and put it online;
- arrange the same results as a **dashboard**.

. . .

**You've built the two axes:** one document to a branded PDF (Day 1), one folder to a published site
(Day 2), with yesterday's report now a page of it. Everything your **team project** needs.

::: notes
- **Close on the report:** the strongest line here is that the document they wrote yesterday is a page
  of the site they built today. Everything else on this slide is machinery.
:::

## Demos (if time) {#demos}

Extra topics:

::: {.incremental}
- **Book versus website** — mostly the same machinery. Pick a **book** when you need one linear read with
  global numbering, a **website** otherwise. *(1 decision, not a new toolset.)*
- **Interactivity** — an **htmlwidget** (`plotly`, `leaflet`) is pure R and self-contained. **OJS**
  *(Observable JS, a browser-side, non-R path)* and **Shinylive** *(Shiny running in the browser,
  no server)* are links, not live builds.
:::

::: notes
- **Timing:** cut-able tail — trim from the bottom if under ~5 min left; all watch-me, nothing built live.
- **Dashboards used to be a bullet here.** They are now a lab step (Part 2, "Ship a dashboard"), so
  this slide no longer covers them. If the room ran out of time and nobody got there, the rendered
  [dashboard](../../labs/quarto-projects/dashboard.qmd){target="_blank"} is still worth 30 seconds:
  name the four regions — two valueboxes across the top, a card with the boxplot, and a two-tab panel.
:::
